Tort law (from the Latin tortus, "twisted", "wry", meaning "wrong" or "injury") is a body of law that addresses civil wrongs that harm others, their property, their business, or their reputation.
Tort claims have four elements: a prima facie breach of duty, a reasonably foreseeable plaintiff, a reasonably foreseeable wrongful action, and damage.
The one who commits the tortious act is called a tortfeasor.
Most modern tort cases are settled through claims adjustment and defended by insurance lawyers. Some cases, however, go to trial, and the decision of the court is recorded as a precedent. Interpretation of these precedents is the responsibility of the courts in later cases.
One of the most important distinguishing features of torts is that, unlike some other areas of the law, the liability of the person who commits the tort is not waived by written agreement between the parties.
The two most common forms of tortious injury are intentional torts and negligent torts. Intentional torts occur when someone intentionally affects someone else's well-being or property. Negligent torts occur when someone fails to exercise the degree of care that society expects to protect other people or their property.
Negligence is a tort because it involves the breach of a duty to exercise reasonable care, and the standard for determining liability is based on whether a reasonable person would have exercised such care. A negligence claim is not actionable unless the plaintiff can demonstrate that the defendant had a duty of care to the plaintiff under the circumstances, that the defendant breached that duty, and that the damages were the proximate cause of the breach.
Common law courts began shifting toward a no-liability regime for products, except for fraud or breach of express warranty, by developing the doctrine of caveat emptor (buyer beware) in the early 1600's. The decision in Winterbottom v. Wright (1842), which allowed actions against railway companies, was one of the first cases in which strict liability for defective products was imposed. However, strict liability for products was not adopted in the United States until the twentieth century.
The first step toward modern product liability law was MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (1916), a landmark New York case in which the court held that a manufacturer is liable in tort when a defective product or unreasonably dangerous condition unreasonably dangerous condition exists in the product when it left the hands of the manufacturer, and if the manufacturer knows that it will be used without inspection for defects. Also in 1916, the Uniform Union, was promulgated by the National Commission on Uniform State Laws to provide states with a model for strict liability. All states adopted a version of the Uniform Act by 1965.
The most significant development in product liability law was the 1963 California Supreme Court case Greenman v. Yuba Power Products, Inc., which was the third step in abandoning the strict liability for products based on the English case Rylands v. Fletcher (1860), which held that "anyone who for his own purposes brings on his lands and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril, and, if he does not do so, is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape."
The Greenman case was the first to impose strict liability for defective products, without the need to prove negligence or strict liability for defective products, in addition to holding that the product seller was strictly liable, regardless of whether it was the manufacturer or not.
The Restatement codified the Greenman doctrine in Section 402(A) (1964). The 1969 California Supreme Court case Greenman v. B. Lord Co. concluded that such defendants are liable to direct customers and users, as well as to innocent bystanders who are randomly injured by defective products.
The U.S. Supreme Court upheld strict liability for products in 1986 in the case of Saxon v. L. Boring Co. and adopted the doctrine as part of federal admiralty law. The 1990 case of In re "E.R.," the court overturned the California Supreme Court's 1986 decision in Greenman v. B. Lord Co. and held that strict liability does not apply to repair shops, even if they are liable for breach of an express warranty.
The North Carolina legislature enacted a statute expressly banning strict liability for defective products in 1995, and the state's court of appeals upheld the statute in 2015. As of 2018, the five states that have rejected strict liability are Delaware, Massachusetts, Michigan, North Carolina, and Virginia.
In 1993, a report of the American Law Institute proposed that the strict liability doctrine be abolished. In 2015, however, the Supreme Court of New Jersey reversed the state's highest court ruling in Henningsen v. Bloomfield Motors, Inc., which had abolished strict liability for defective design and manufacture, and reinstated the doctrine.
Tort claims typically seek compensation for injury to a person, property, reputation, or economic interest. The plaintiff must demonstrate that the actions or lack of action was the legally recognizable cause of the harm, that is, the plaintiff must prove that the defendant's actions or lack of action were the cause of the harm. Examples of tort claims include battery, negligence, and defamation.
Negligent torts have four elements: duty, breach of duty, cause, and damages. A person has a duty to act as a reasonable person would act under similar circumstances. A person breaches their duty when they fail to act in the way that a reasonable person would act under similar circumstances. The breaching person must have been the cause of the harm, which is the legal injury. Damages are the harm suffered by the injured party, which may include monetary loss, pain and suffering, and loss of property or reputation.
A person who commits a tortious act is called a tortfeasor. A person who suffers the harm may sue the tortfeasor for damages. The tortfeasor may have an affirmative defense, such as assumption of risk, that reduces or eliminates the liability for damages.
Tort liability is not necessarily the same as liability under contract law. As such, tort law generally comprises a separate set of causes of action. Tort law acknowledges that there may be a duty arising from a written contract, but the basis for any liability under the contract remains a tort. Similarly, liability arising from crimes such as murder, manslaughter, or theft may also be torts, although they are separate from tort law.
Strict liability is a legal standard that holds a person liable for the consequences of his or her action without a finding of fault, negligence, or intent. It is sometimes contrasted with tort law, where intentional wrongdoing may lead to punitive damages.
Strict liability can be imposed on those who handle hazardous materials, professional malpractice, and defective products that enter the stream of commerce. In the case of consumer products, Article 2 of the United States Uniform commercial code allows a buyer to sue a seller for damages caused by a defect that existed when the item left the seller's control. In cases of strict liability, the defendant can raise a defense of absence of fault, in an attempt to escape liability, but may not rely on the plaintiff's contributory fault as an excuse for escaping liability.
The liability insurance industry has had an important role in developing tort law. In the late 19 th century, the insurance industry imposed negligence and strict liability as means of discharging the duty to settle insured tort losses. In the United States, state courts led the evolution of tort law, with an important role played by the Restatement of Law (American Law Institute 1932-1978), which provided analysis of many common law cases, including tort, negligence, and strict liability cases. In 1932, the United States Supreme Court adopted the Restatement (second edition) in the case of United States v. Standard Products Co., along with the doctrine of market-share liability.
In 1969, the California Supreme Court held that such defendants are liable to direct customers and users, as well as to innocent bystanders who are randomly injured by defective products. In 1970, the courts of California, New Jersey, and New York adopted the strict liability concept in product liability cases.
In 1986, the United States Supreme Court upheld strict liability for defective products as part of federal admiralty law, and in 1993, a report of the American Law Institute proposed to abolish the strict liability doctrine. In 2015, however, the Supreme Court of New Jersey reversed the state's highest court ruling in Henningsen v. Bloomfield Motors, Inc., which had abolished strict liability for defective design and manufacture, and reinstated the doctrine.
Tort claims in the United States are usually processed by the state courts, including those that have exclusive or concurrent jurisdiction for that type of claim. The claimant need only prove that the tort occurred and that the defendant was responsible. The defendant can then raise a defense of absence of fault, which may eliminate or reduce liability.
The early history of tort law can be traced back to the twelfth century, when courts began to hear personal injury cases under writs of trespass. In 1401, the English case Beaulieu v Finglam imposed strict liability for the escape of fire, and in 1580, the practice of allowing juries to settle personal injury disputes was extended in England.
In 1842, the English case of Winterbottom v Wright exemplifies the privity of contract defense. The plaintiff was a mail coach driver who contracted with the postal service to deliver mail. The plaintiff was injured when the axle of the coach broke and he sued the maker of the axle. The court ruled that the post office could sue the maker but that the plaintiff could not because the plaintiff had no contractual relationship with the manufacturer. In 1842, the English case of Henningsen v. Hindered involved the claimant's unsuccessful attempt to sue a bar for serving liquor to the claimant's drunken husband.

The Texas Legislature is set to begin its special session on July 19. One of the crucial issues that will be considered is whether to extend the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force, which is set to expire unless lawmakers act.
Task force extension should be on the special session agenda, because Texas has to fix how it counts maternal deaths. In 2020, the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force – an expert group of physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts who review individual maternal deaths case by case – found that the state’s “maternal death rates are even higher than previous estimates” published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the state health department.
The task force launched in 2013, at a time when Texas was already known as a “dangerous place to have a baby.” Since that point, Texas has struggled to make improvements in the number of mothers and infants who die in the state, an issue that disproportionately affects Black women. In Texas, Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at far higher rates than white or Hispanic women.
Black women are especially vulnerable to reproductive health disparities. One study found that Black women in the United States are twice as likely to die during pregnancy or childbirth as white women, and up to four times as likely to die during pregnancy when compared to white women in other developed countries.
Another study published in 2020, found that Black women in Texas face “a significant disparity” in maternal deaths. The researchers identified in their study an “increase from 2012 to 2014 in the rate of maternal deaths.” They reported that, “the CDC definition of pregnancy-related deaths extends the period to one year from the resolution of the pregnancy. Therefore, it is possible that if states do not include all pregnancy-related deaths in their calculations, the number of cases included may vary over time.”
Texas does not include all pregnancy-related deaths in its calculations. The Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force includes all pregnancy-related deaths, and it’s this crucial task that needs to be extended.
Errors within the Texas data included problems with how pregnancy was recorded on death certificates. These omissions, together with undercounting and misclassification, distorted the true extent of maternal deaths. For example, a 2020 study found that when a death was labeled “cardiac arrest” it could reveal that the woman had weeks of untreated hypertension. The failure to include death certificate information related to pregnancy, or to include the death certificate at all, means that the maternal death rate in Texas is likely to be even higher than previously thought.
The Texas Task Force’s early analysis found that Black women accounted for about one in nine births in the state but nearly three in ten maternal deaths. Their review identified direct obstetric causes that range from severe bleeding to obstructed labor, for which highly effective interventions exist. Texas has to fix how it counts maternal deaths.

By 2011, only 30 states and the District of Colorado had implemented the new standard death certificate, and only eight included the question on maternal mortality.

Some states don’t wait until September 1, but postpone their effective date to the first day of a new legislative session. Under current practice, most bills get an effective date of September 1 in odd-numbered years. If our elected officials are serious about protecting Texas women and their infants, then they need to get to work. Now.
The issue of maternal mortality is not only a health issue – it is an economic, civil rights, and social issue, too. It is an important marker of a country’s overall health, and it reflects its health infrastructure.

The human language is an invention. An invention like the wheel and the nail. We use words to gather, to communicate, to understand and to express. We use words to build bridges of understanding and to build walls to keep one another out.
Words can be beautiful when they hold you up. Words can be frightening when they fall. Words have power to make and to mend.
You have two ears and one mouth. Listen more than you talk. Every word is a chosen word. They are not without importance. They are not without consequence. They are not without cost.
My friend. My love. My child. My God.
Like the vastness of the universe, each word has a variety of uses and meanings. The complexity of the feelings involved makes love unusually difficult to define consistently compared to other emotional states. It is sometimes defined in terms of interpersonal relationships, with such distinctions as romantic love, parental love and platonic love. In 1970, psychologist Robert Sternberg developed a theory called the triangular theory of love. He proposed that there are three components of love: intimacy, passion and commitment. According to Sternberg’s theory, the combination of these three components forms six different kinds of love relationships. The form of love can vary from person to person.
Love is an action. Love is an activity. Love is a project. Love is a verb.
Chosen words live in the space between people. They live in the territory of trust, risk and promise. Love as a verb has consequences. Ambiguity in the actions of love can leave doubt. Cooking. Driving across town. Remembering birthdays. These actions can leave doubt in their expressions. For love’s virtue represents human kindness, compassion and affection, as “the unselfish loyal and benevolent concern for the good of another.”
An apology can be mimed with a bowed head. A hand on a shoulder can say “I’m sorry.” Love can be expressed with a gesture, a glance, or a good deed. Actions of love can be ambiguous. Like cooking, driving across town, and remembering birthdays. These actions can leave doubt in their expressions.
Today, I resolve to say these words more often. I resolve to not trust the hands of others to do the work of the mouth. I resolve to stop and think about the words I am speaking. And I resolve to not just say them but to mean them. To mean them with every vibration in my body.
I am a belief. I am a feeling. I am a thought. I am a prayer. I am a condition. But, I am not a word. No. I am not a word.
And I know that my words are not so much what I tell the world as what I will to the world. For my words are not separate from myself. They are the expression of my deepest most honest sentiments, my profoundest desires, my most liberal sympathies, my noblest aspirations.
They are not a sound that I may control. My words are an action that I may express. For words are not a set of vocal noises that I may constrain. My words are an experience that I may share. My words are an experience that I may share.
If you wish for a word, a word for your love. Consider these:
Love. Hello. Help or Danger. Believe or Trust. Peace. Friend. Forgive. Always.
The word “love” has a variety of related but distinct meanings in different contexts. Many other languages use multiple words for concepts that are denoted as “love” in English. Ancient Greek has eight words for love:
Agape, for universal love; Eros, for romantic love; Philia, for deep friendship; Storge, for familial love; Xenia, for hospitality and guest friendship; Pre, for first love; Philautia, for self-love; Agape, for love in general.
In Arabic, the word “Would” is used for love of a mother, the word “Hybridization” for love of a spouse, and the word “Shame” for love of food.
Trust is an experience that I may share.

Since then, bubbles have been generally associated with stock exchanges and financial markets in general and, although there have been notable exceptions, the term has been most commonly applied to the stock market.
There are two main types of bubbles, equity bubbles and debt bubbles. While both result in a mispricing of assets, the distinction lies in the type of asset being mispriced. In an equity bubble, the prices of tangible assets rise far beyond their fundamentals, often due to the illusory promise of future profits. As the price rises, more people are encouraged to join the market and new wealth is generated. The bubble continues to grow so long as people believe that the high prices of the assets will continue to rise. In a debt bubble, investors put their capital in intangible or credit-based investments with little ability to satisfy growing demand in a non-existent market. When the bubble bursts, the tangible assets that have been used as collateral to borrow and invest become worthless. As a result, many borrowers are unable to repay and the lenders are forced to pull back, resulting in a forced selling of assets that pushes prices down even further.

Self-assessment of knowledge or ability is not easy. It takes a fair amount of metacognitive skill to know how much we know or what we can do. And people are usually more accurate when they predict their raw score than when they assess their performance relative to their peer group. There are strategies, however, to improve our self-assessments and to develop metacognitive skills. Here we review a selection of strategies to promote metacognition and then we will explore research that has tried to answer the question, “What are we good at?”
The link between metacognition and self-assessment
Metacognition generally has two components: knowledge about cognition and regulation of cognition. Knowledge about cognition is what we know about learning and thinking. Regulation of cognition is using that knowledge to guide our actions. For example, planning how to approach a learning task, monitoring comprehension, and evaluating progress toward completing a task are all metacognitive skills. People with high metacognitive knowledge and skill are able to identify the blocks to learning early on and change tools or strategies to ensure goal attainment. They are self-regulated learners who know how to use the “right tool for the job” and modify their learning strategies and skills based on their awareness of effectiveness. This increases their ability to set and maintain learning goals. Through careful planning, self-regulated learners are able to bring their knowledge of learning and their understanding of their cognitive task to bear on a particular learning goal.
Flavell defined metacognition as knowledge about cognition and control of cognition. More recently, for purposes of assessing the development of metacognition, the term “executive management processes” has been used to denote the kinds of processes that involve planning, monitoring, evaluating, and revising one’s own thinking processes and products. These processes operate on the knowledge and beliefs that people have about how they think, learn, and remember.
People are usually better at estimating their performance on single questions than on whole exams, because time affects forgetting. People are not better at predicting which questions they will answer correctly, but they are better at predicting which questions they will answer incorrectly. Surveys of exam readiness may ask students to estimate how well they will do, to list which topics they are most confident about and which topics they are least confident about, and to write down one example of a concept we haven’t discussed. These kinds of prompts can help students plan their studies and identify gaps in their knowledge.

The testing effect
The testing effect, also known as retrieval practice, active recall, practice testing, or test-enhanced learning, is the finding that retrieval practice (recalling information from memory rather than re-studying it) is superior to restudying the material. The most prominent alternative explanation is that the effect is mainly a statistical artifact of regression toward the mean combined with the better-than-average effect.
The most consistent demonstration of the testing effect is when tests or quizzes are given after class during a review session or as homework. These are the kinds of tests that students often perceive as a waste of time, but they are a powerful form of retrieval practice, and they can be used to increase knowledge retention. Less common are pre-test retrieval practices, where students are asked to produce information at the start of a course or unit. These pre-tests can be used to get greater results. While a pre-exam survey can ask students which topics they feel most and least confident about, a pre-test asks students to recall as much as they can about a topic at the outset. What this does is provide a record of what students have learned before they’ve had time to forget, so teachers can adjust instruction.
The benefit is greater when the test is more challenging for memory. This means that simply re-studying the material and/or highlighting textbook passages is not nearly as beneficial as testing yourself. When students studied without a test, they forgot about 384 percent of the information, but when they made a test, they forgot about 2013 percent of the information.
